What may you do?","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"Turn right carefully after yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03"]},"rationale":{"text":"A green arrow beside red allows careful travel only in the arrow's direction, after yielding to others.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signals and what they mean","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Officers come before signals.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Red, yellow, green, and arrows.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the section on signals, signs, and markers with traffic lights. Signals look simple, but each color and each flashing or steady version asks something different of you. Before any light, there is one rule above the rest: when a police officer directs traffic, the officer's direction comes first. Then we will go through steady and flashing red, steady and flashing yellow, the flashing yellow left arrow, steady green, and green arrows. Practice questions often swap the flashing and steady versions, so we will compare them side by side as we go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Officers and steady red","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Obey signals unless an officer directs.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]},{"text":"Steady red: stop before the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]},{"text":"Lawful turns only, after yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"You obey every traffic signal unless a police officer directs you otherwise, and an officer's order stands even when it differs from the usual rule. At a steady red light, stop before the crosswalk, or before the intersection if there is no crosswalk. After stopping, you may make a lawful right turn, or a left turn from one one-way street onto another one-way street. Whenever you turn on red, yield to pedestrians and to other vehicles already lawfully in the intersection. If no turn is allowed, wait for the light to change before you go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Flashing red and yellow","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Flashing red: stop, then go safely.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Steady yellow: stop safely or clear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Flashing yellow: slow with caution.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"A flashing red light means stop completely, then go when it is safe, much like a stop sign, while cross traffic may keep moving. A steady yellow light means the signal is about to turn red. Stop if you can do so safely, or clear the intersection with caution if you cannot. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution. A flashing yellow left-turn arrow lets you turn left, but you must yield to oncoming traffic first. Notice how flashing red and flashing yellow ask for very different actions from the driver.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Green lights and arrows","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady green: go, watching the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Green arrow beside red: arrow direction only.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Plain green left: yield to oncoming.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"A steady green light lets you go straight or turn, but you still watch the intersection for anyone who has not cleared it. If you turn left on a plain green light, you yield to all oncoming traffic. A green arrow beside a red light lets you go carefully only in the direction of the arrow, after yielding to anyone already in the intersection or crosswalk. So green never means go without looking. It means you may move, and the arrow, when there is one, tells you exactly which way you may move while the rest of the signal stays red.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Steady or flashing","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady red: stop and wait.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Flashing red: stop, then go safely.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Steady yellow stops; flashing yellow slows.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from steady and flashing lights. Steady red means stop and wait, with only lawful turns allowed after stopping. Flashing red means stop fully and then go when it is safe, with no need to wait for a change. Steady yellow means a red is coming, so stop if you safely can. Flashing yellow means slow down and go ahead with caution. Learners often treat flashing red like a slowdown, or flashing yellow like a stop. When a question names a light, first ask whether it is steady or flashing, then pick the matching action.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the green arrow","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red ball, green right arrow.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"What may you do?","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you reach an intersection where the signal shows a red ball with a green arrow pointing right. What may you do? Work out your answer before reading on. You may turn right carefully, after yielding to anyone already in the intersection or crosswalk. You may not go straight or turn left, because the arrow only allows travel in its own direction while the rest of the signal is red. If the arrow were a flashing yellow left arrow instead, you could turn left, but only after yielding to oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Signals in brief","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Officers override signals.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Flashing red stops; flashing yellow slows.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Arrows allow only their direction.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Obey every signal unless an officer directs you otherwise. At steady red, stop before the crosswalk or intersection, and make only lawful turns after yielding. At flashing red, stop fully, then go when safe. At steady yellow, stop if you safely can or clear with caution. At flashing yellow, slow down with caution, and at a flashing yellow left arrow, turn only after yielding to oncoming cars. Steady green lets you go with care, plain green lefts yield to oncoming traffic, and green arrows beside red allow careful travel in the arrow's direction. Next, sign colors and shapes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Sign colors and shapes","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Signs use colors and shapes so drivers can recognize their meaning before they can read the words.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Knowing what each kind of sign does helps you react the right way to it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Far ahead, Raj sees an orange diamond sign that he cannot yet read.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Orange marks construction and maintenance, and a diamond warns of a hazard.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},"result":{"text":"Raj slows down and gets ready for a work zone before he can read the words.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a yellow sign gives an order that must be obeyed like a regulation.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"correction":{"text":"Yellow signs warn of hazards; black and white signs carry regulations, and red ones order stops, yields, or posted orders.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Octagon stop, triangle yield, diamond warns.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A blue sign appears beside the highway. What kind of information does it give?","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"answer":{"text":"Motorist services.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"Blue signs point to motorist services, while green shows allowed moves and direction and brown shows recreation.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"The language of signs","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"What signs do.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Colors and shapes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic signs speak a language of their own. Long before you can read a sign's words, its color and shape tell you what kind of message it carries. In this lesson we will look at the four jobs signs do, the meaning of each sign color, and the meaning of each sign shape. Then we will pair colors with shapes so you can recognize a sign at a glance. This is one of the most useful skills for the road, because it gives you extra time to react, especially to stop, yield, and warning signs that ask you to change what you are doing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What signs do","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Warn of hidden hazards.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Guide travelers along routes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Inform and regulate.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic signs have four main jobs. They warn of hazards ahead that you may not be able to see yet. They guide travelers along routes so you can find your way. They publish local rules and customs so you know what is expected. And they regulate speed and movement, telling you what you must or must not do. Keeping these jobs in mind helps you sort any sign you meet: is it warning you, guiding you, informing you, or giving you an order? The answer tells you how seriously to take the sign and what to do about it. Sorting first makes the details easier to recall.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Colors and shapes","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red stops, yellow warns, orange works.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Octagon stop, triangle yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Diamond warns, pentagon marks schools.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Each color has a meaning. Red is for stop, yield, or posted orders. Green shows allowed moves and direction. Blue marks motorist services. Yellow warns. Black and white carry regulations. Orange marks construction and maintenance, and brown marks recreation and scenery. Shapes have meanings too. An octagon is used only for stop signs, and a triangle only for yield. A pennant gives advance notice of a no-passing zone, a diamond warns of hazards, a vertical rectangle carries regulations, a horizontal rectangle guides, a pentagon marks school zones and crossings, and a circle warns of a railroad ahead.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Warning versus regulation","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow diamond: a warning.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Black and white rectangle: a regulation.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Red octagon: stop only.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from sign types. Yellow signs, often diamonds, warn you about something ahead, such as a curve or a crossing. They ask you to pay attention and slow down, and ignoring them can still be a violation. Black and white signs, usually vertical rectangles, are regulations, and they carry the force of law. Red marks stops, yields, and posted orders, and the red octagon is used only for stop signs. If the sign were brown, it would point to recreation or scenery, and if it were orange, it would mark construction or maintenance ahead. The color alone tells you what kind of help or warning to expect from it. Color is often the first clue you see from a distance, so learn the code well.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Colors and shapes in brief","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signs warn, guide, inform, regulate.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Each color has one meaning.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Octagon stop, triangle yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, signs warn of hidden hazards, guide travelers, publish local rules, and regulate speed and movement. These signs alert you to things you may not see in time: a signal around a bend, a low underpass, a divided highway starting or ending, lanes being added or dropped, curves and winding stretches, side roads, rough or wet pavement, and crossing traffic. Each one asks you to adjust before you reach the hazard. Each warning has its own instruction: compare an underpass clearance with your load, watch traffic in a newly added lane, and follow the stated directions for the particular curve or other hazard ahead.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Early warnings","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signal ahead and low clearance.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Divided highway begins; added lane.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Reverse curves, side roads, rough road.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Early warning signs flag a signal ahead, an underpass with limited clearance for tall loads, the start of a divided highway with a median, an added lane that needs no merge, reverse curves turning right then left, a side road joining, a rough road surface, and crossing traffic. Follow each sign’s own instruction. For a reverse curve, reduce speed, stay right and avoid passing; that instruction does not apply to every warning. An added lane is the one warning in this group that eases the road rather than tightening it, since traffic joining in its own lane does not need to merge into yours.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"More road warnings","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sharp turns and winding roads.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Divided highway ends; wet roads.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Crossroads and lane reductions.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Other warnings flag a sharp turn shown by an arrow, a winding road, and the end of a divided highway, where two-way traffic returns. On a wet road warning, avoid sudden moves. Keep to the right lane, because oncoming cars will be on your left once the highway is no longer divided. A gradual curve is shown by an arrow too. A crossroads warning means you should look in all directions, and a lane reduction warning means the number of lanes is shrinking ahead, so be ready to adjust your position before the road narrows rather than at the last moment.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Every curve, same response","fact_ids":["sec05-R05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Reverse curve, sharp turn: slow.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Winding road, gradual curve: slow.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Follow each sign’s specific instructions.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that hides in plain sight. Curve warnings come in several forms: a reverse curve, a sharp turn, a winding road, and a gradual curve. Do not assume every description gives the same set of instructions. Reverse curves, sharp turns and gradual curves call for slowing, keeping right and no passing. The winding-road description says to drive slowly and carefully without passing. A question may name any one of these signs, so identify the sign first. If the road also became wet, you would avoid sudden moves. And if a lane reduction warning followed, you would be ready to adjust your position early. Each warning gives you time, and the safe use of that time is to slow down and plan.
